t: Solemnity of the Octave of Christmas
b: Eight days after Christmas the Church names Mary Theotokos, 'God-bearer', the title the Council of Ephesus (431) defended: the child she bore is God. The day is also the World Day of Peace and the feast of the circumcision and naming of Jesus (Luke 2:21).

n: Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen
t: Bishops and Doctors of the Church
b: Two friends from student days in Athens who became the great theologians of the Trinity against Arianism. Basil organised monastic life in the East and built a hospital city for the poor; Gregory, 'the Theologian', preached the five orations on the divinity of Christ that shaped the Creed.

n: The Most Holy Name of Jesus
b: 'Thou shalt call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins' (Matt 1:21). The devotion to the Name spread through Bernardine of Siena, who carried the monogram IHS through the cities of Italy. Also remembered today: Saint Genevieve, the shepherdess who saved Paris from Attila by prayer.

A New York widow with five children who entered the Catholic Church in 1805 at great social cost, founded the Sisters of Charity and the first free Catholic school for girls in America. The first native-born citizen of the United States to be canonised (1975).

A Bohemian who came to America because his own diocese had too many priests, walked the frontier of upstate New York as a missionary, joined the Redemptorists, and as bishop of Philadelphia built the first diocesan school system in the country. He spoke eight languages so that immigrants could confess in their own.

t: Solemnity (kept on the nearest Sunday in many countries)
b: The manifestation of Christ to the nations: the Magi following the star to Bethlehem, and by ancient tradition also his baptism in the Jordan and the wedding at Cana. Older than Christmas in the East, the feast closes the Twelve Days.

A Catalan canon lawyer who compiled the Decretals for Pope Gregory IX, became master general of the Dominicans, and encouraged Thomas Aquinas to write the Summa contra Gentiles for the conversion of the Moors. He lived to be a hundred. Patron of lawyers.

A mysterious monk who appeared on the Danube as the Roman Empire collapsed, organised food for starving towns, negotiated with barbarian kings, and foretold the rise of Odoacer. His disciples carried his body to Naples when they fled.

An African-born abbot who twice refused the see of Canterbury and instead accompanied Theodore of Tarsus to England, where for forty years he ran the school at Canterbury that taught Greek, Latin, astronomy and Scripture to the English Church.

Younger brother of Basil the Great, the most philosophical of the Cappadocian Fathers. His Life of Moses reads the Exodus as the soul's endless ascent into God — 'to find God is to seek him without end.' Called 'father of fathers' by the Second Council of Nicaea.

Founder of a great monastery near Bethlehem with hospitals for the sick, the aged and the mentally ill, and churches where Greeks, Armenians and Bessians each prayed in their own language. He defied the emperor Anastasius over the Council of Chalcedon and lived to 105.

Steward at the court of King David of Scotland, then a Cistercian monk and abbot of Rievaulx in Yorkshire, where he ruled six hundred monks with a gentleness that made him 'the Bernard of the North'. His treatise Spiritual Friendship is the medieval classic on friendship in Christ.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: A married pagan philosopher who found God in the opening of John's Gospel, was made bishop of Poitiers, and was exiled to Phrygia for refusing to condemn Athanasius. There he wrote On the Trinity, the first great Latin defence of the divinity of Christ. 'The Athanasius of the West.'

A priest of Nola tortured in the Decian persecution and hidden, legend says, by a spider's web spun over the mouth of his hiding place. He refused a bishopric and gave away his land to the poor; Paulinus of Nola wrote a poem for his feast every year for fourteen years.

Fled the Decian persecution into the Egyptian desert about 250 and lived there ninety years, fed by a raven, according to Jerome's Life of Paul. Anthony the Great found him at the end and buried him in the cloak of Athanasius; two lions, the story says, dug the grave.

Elected after a four-year vacancy under Diocletian, he reorganised the Roman Church into parishes and insisted on penance for those who had apostatised in the persecution. The resulting riots led the emperor Maxentius to banish him; tradition says he was condemned to work as a stable groom.

Hearing 'Go, sell what thou hast, and give to the poor' read in church, a young Egyptian farmer did exactly that and went into the desert, where he fought demons, counselled emperors by letter, and lived to 105. Athanasius's Life of Anthony converted Augustine and set Europe's monasteries in motion.

Daughter of King Béla IV, promised to God before birth if Hungary were delivered from the Mongols. She refused two royal marriages, took the veil on the Danube island that now bears her name, and chose the hardest work of the convent. Also today: the Chair of Peter (traditional calendar).

A Danish king who built churches, protected the poor and levied a tithe for the clergy, and was murdered by rebels at the altar of St Alban's church in Odense. The first Dane to be canonised. Also today: Saints Marius, Martha and their sons, Persian martyrs at Rome.

Fabian, a layman chosen pope when a dove settled on his head, died in the Decian persecution of 250. Sebastian, a Roman officer of the Praetorian guard, was shot with arrows for his faith, nursed back to health by Irene, and clubbed to death when he confronted Diocletian — the arrows made him the most painted of martyrs.

A Roman girl of about twelve who refused marriage and sacrifice under Diocletian and was killed by the sword. Her name sounds like agnus, lamb: on her feast two lambs are blessed in Rome whose wool becomes the pallia of archbishops. Ambrose, Jerome and Augustine all preached about her.

Deacon of Saragossa, tortured on the rack and the gridiron at Valencia under Diocletian; his composure so shook his judge Dacian that the story of it spread through the whole Church. Augustine said his passion was read 'in every land under the sun'. Patron of vintners.

A Franciscan sister of Syracuse, New York, who answered the king of Hawaii's plea for nurses when fifty other congregations had refused, and spent thirty-five years among the lepers of Molokai, promising her sisters they would never catch the disease. None did.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: Bishop of Geneva who could not enter his own Calvinist city, so he slid leaflets under doors — the first religious tracts — and won back the Chablais by gentleness. His Introduction to the Devout Life taught laypeople that holiness is for everyone. Patron of writers and journalists.

On the road to Damascus, breathing threats, Saul of Tarsus was knocked to the ground by a light and a voice: 'Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?' Three days blind, then baptised by Ananias, he became the apostle to the Gentiles. The Week of Prayer for Christian Unity ends today.

Paul's two closest lieutenants and the recipients of three of his letters. Timothy, half Greek and half Jew, was left in charge of Ephesus; Titus, a Greek, of Crete. Tradition says Timothy was beaten to death for opposing a festival of Diana, and Titus died old in Gortyna.

A Franciscan tertiary of Brescia who gathered unmarried women to teach girls in their own homes — the Ursulines, the first teaching order of women, founded thirty years before Trent and without cloister, a scandal in her century.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: The 'dumb ox' of Aquino whose Summa Theologiae is the cathedral of medieval thought. His family imprisoned him to stop him joining the Dominicans; he escaped, studied under Albert the Great, and wrote until a vision at Mass made him say 'all I have written seems like straw'. He died on the way to the Council of Lyon.

A British monk whose furious sermon On the Ruin of Britain is almost the only written witness to the century when the Saxons conquered the island — the age Arthurian legend remembers. He ended his days as a hermit on an island off Brittany.

A Roman deacon's daughter martyred under Alexander Severus; her relics were found beneath the Forum in 1634 and Bernini's Santi Luca e Martina was built over them. Also today: Hyacintha Mariscotti, the vain nun who became an ascetic and founder of confraternities for the poor.

A Piedmontese peasant's son who learned juggling to draw boys to catechism, and in industrial Turin gathered the street children into an oratory where they were fed, taught a trade and loved. 'Don Bosco' founded the Salesians, now the second-largest religious order in the world.

A slave's daughter who, legend says, gave away her father's sword to a beggar, founded the double monastery of Kildare where a perpetual fire burned for a thousand years, and became with Patrick and Columba a patron of Ireland. The rush cross woven on her eve still hangs in Irish homes.

wp: Presentation of Jesus at the Temple
b: Forty days after his birth Jesus is carried into the Temple, and old Simeon takes him in his arms: 'a light to the revelation of the Gentiles.' Candles are blessed and carried in procession — Candlemas — and the Christmas cycle finally closes.

A physician-bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, said to have saved a boy choking on a fishbone; hence the blessing of throats with crossed candles on his day. Martyred under Licinius by being torn with iron wool-combs. Also today: Ansgar, apostle of Scandinavia.

A wild Florentine youth converted by his mother's reproach, he became a Carmelite, bishop of Fiesole, and the peacemaker of Tuscany's warring factions. Also today: John de Brito, Portuguese Jesuit martyred in India in 1693 for refusing to leave his converts.

A Sicilian noblewoman of Catania who refused the consul Quintianus and was tortured, her breasts cut off, under Decius. Her veil is carried against eruptions of Etna. Named in the Roman Canon of the Mass with Agnes, Cecilia, Lucy and Anastasia.

Twenty-six Christians — Jesuits, Franciscans and laymen, three of them boys — crucified on a hill above Nagasaki after being marched six hundred miles through winter. Paul Miki, a Japanese Jesuit, preached forgiveness from his cross. Two centuries later missionaries found the hidden Christians still keeping the faith.

A young Ravenna nobleman who watched his father kill a man in a duel and fled to a monastery in horror; he spent his life founding hermitages that joined the solitude of the desert to the common life. 'Sit in your cell as in paradise.' (Kept on June 19 in the new calendar.)

Kidnapped in Darfur at seven, sold five times, scarred by her owners, she was brought to Italy, learned of Christ from the Canossian sisters and refused to go back to Sudan — an Italian court ruled she was free. She spent fifty years as a humble sister in Schio. Patroness of Sudan and of victims of trafficking. Also today: Jerome Emiliani.

An aged deaconess of Alexandria seized by a mob that broke her teeth, then threatened her with fire unless she blasphemed; she asked a moment as if to consider, and leapt into the flames. Invoked against toothache. Bishop Dionysius, who knew her, tells the story.

Twin sister of Benedict, and a nun near Monte Cassino. At their last yearly meeting she begged him to stay the night talking of heaven; when he refused, she prayed, and a storm broke so violent he could not leave. Three days later he saw her soul rise as a dove. Gregory the Great tells it: 'she who loved more, could do more.'

t: Optional memorial · World Day of the Sick
b: On 11 February 1858 a fourteen-year-old peasant girl, Bernadette Soubirous, saw a lady in a grotto by the Gave who later said, 'I am the Immaculate Conception' — words the child did not understand. Millions have since drunk from the spring; the Church has recognised seventy cures as miraculous.

n: The Seven Founders of the Servite Order
b: Seven Florentine cloth merchants who left their businesses in 1233 to live in penance on Monte Senario, and founded the Servants of Mary, devoted to her sorrows. The last of them, Alexis Falconieri, lived to 110. (Kept on February 17 in the new calendar.)

A Dominican nun of Prato who for twelve years relived the Passion every week from Thursday noon to Friday afternoon, corresponded with three future popes, and reformed her convent with practical good sense. Philip Neri, who never left Rome, is said to have conversed with her in a vision.

t: Bishop; monk — apostles of the Slavs, patrons of Europe
b: Two brothers from Thessalonica who translated the Scriptures and the liturgy into Slavonic, inventing an alphabet to do it, and defended a Slavic liturgy before the pope against German bishops who allowed only Hebrew, Greek and Latin. Also today: Valentine, the martyr-priest of Rome.

Spiritual director of Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial, who believed her visions of the Sacred Heart when no one else did; later chaplain to the Duchess of York in London, imprisoned in the Popish Plot, and sent home to die at forty-one.

The slave of Philemon who fled to Paul in prison and was sent back with the shortest letter in the New Testament — 'receive him as myself.' Tradition makes him bishop of Ephesus after Timothy and a martyr at Rome. Also today: Juliana of Nicomedia, virgin martyr.

n: Alexis Falconieri and the Seven Holy Founders
b: See February 12 in the traditional calendar: seven merchants of Florence who became the Servants of Mary. Alexis alone refused the priesthood and begged for the community's bread. Also today: Finan of Lindisfarne, who baptised the kings of Mercia and the East Saxons.

The girl of Lourdes, who after the apparitions entered the Sisters of Charity at Nevers and was set to work in the infirmary: 'I was a broom Our Lady used; she has put me back in my corner.' She died at thirty-five of tuberculosis of the bone; her body lies incorrupt at Nevers.

A nobleman whose hunting fire got out of control and burned the countryside; when an innocent man was condemned for it, Conrad confessed, paid with his whole fortune, and with his wife's agreement became a Franciscan hermit in Sicily, famous for his gentleness with birds.

Brother and sister, nine and seven, who with their cousin Lúcia saw the Lady at Fatima in 1917. Both died in the influenza epidemic within three years, as she had told them they would; Jacinta offered her lonely hospital death for sinners. The youngest non-martyrs ever canonised.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: An orphan who tended pigs, then a hermit of Fonte Avellana and, against his will, cardinal-bishop of Ostia, the fiercest reformer of a corrupt eleventh-century clergy. Dante places him in the sphere of Saturn among the contemplatives.

Not a relic but an office: the teaching authority of Peter and his successors, celebrated in Rome since the fourth century. 'Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church' (Matt 16:18). Bernini's bronze throne in St Peter's encloses an ancient wooden chair.

A disciple of the apostle John, burned in the stadium of Smyrna at eighty-six: 'Eighty-six years have I served him, and he has done me no wrong; how can I blaspheme my King who saved me?' The account of his death is the oldest martyrdom narrative after Stephen's.

Chosen by lot to replace Judas, 'that he might take part in this ministry and apostleship' (Acts 1:25). Tradition sends him to Ethiopia or Cappadocia and gives him a martyr's death. (Kept on May 14 in the new calendar.)

An English nun, niece of Boniface, who followed him to Germany and ruled the double monastery of Heidenheim. Oil that flows from the rock of her tomb at Eichstätt has been collected for a thousand years. The eve of her May feast gave Walpurgisnacht its name.

A monk of the Egyptian desert made bishop of Gaza, then the most stubbornly pagan city in Palestine. He went to Constantinople and obtained from the empress an order to close the temples; the great temple of Marnas was burned and a church built on its ashes.

t: Monk and Doctor of the Church
b: An Armenian monk whose Book of Lamentations — ninety-five prayers 'speaking with God from the depths of the heart' — is kept under the pillow of the sick in Armenia to this day. Pope Francis named him Doctor of the Church in 2015. Also today: Gabriel Possenti, the young Passionist.

Two brothers who founded the first monasteries in the Jura mountains, Condat and Lauconne, drawing so many that a third had to be built for their sister. Romanus was gentle, Lupicinus severe; between them they filled the forests of Burgundy with monks.

A Dane by blood, bishop of Worcester and archbishop of York, who with Dunstan and Ethelwold revived English monasticism after the Viking wars. He died on his knees, having washed the feet of twelve poor men, as he did every day in Lent.

Founder of the monastery of Menevia (St Davids), where the monks pulled the plough themselves and drank only water — 'David the Waterman'. At the synod of Brefi, legend says, the ground rose under him so that all could hear. His last words: 'Do the little things.'

Brother of Cedd, pupil of Aidan, bishop of the Mercians at Lichfield, who walked everywhere until Archbishop Theodore lifted him bodily onto a horse. Bede loved him: when the wind rose, Chad would stop and pray, 'because the Lord moves the air to remind us of the judgment.'

Heiress of a Philadelphia banking fortune who asked Leo XIII to send missionaries to the Indians, and was told, 'Why not become one yourself?' She founded the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament and spent twenty million dollars on schools for Black and Native Americans, including Xavier University.

Second son of the king of Poland, who refused the Hungarian crown his father tried to win for him by war, wore a hair shirt under his royal robes, and died of tuberculosis at twenty-five. Patron of Poland and Lithuania; the hymn Omni die dic Mariae was found in his coffin.

A Neapolitan noble who joined the Alcantarine Franciscans at sixteen, walked barefoot, slept three hours a night, and was so besieged by the sick of Naples that he had to be protected by the friars. Also today: Piran, the Cornish abbot who floated from Ireland on a millstone.

t: Virgin, reformer of the Poor Clares
b: A carpenter's daughter who lived walled up as an anchoress, then, commanded in a vision by Francis, left her cell to restore the strict rule of Clare; she founded seventeen convents and reconciled the rival popes' followers. She foretold her own death at the hour of Compline.

A young Carthaginian mother of good family and her pregnant slave, thrown to the beasts in the arena on the birthday of the emperor's son. Perpetua's prison diary — the earliest Christian writing by a woman — survives; she guided the gladiator's sword to her own throat. Both are named in the Roman Canon.

A Portuguese soldier, shepherd and bookseller who at forty heard John of Ávila preach and went so mad with remorse that he was locked in an asylum; the cruelty he saw there made him found a hospital in Granada where the sick were treated with mercy. Patron of hospitals and nurses.

A Roman noblewoman who, married at thirteen against her wish, made her palace a refuge for the plague-stricken and the starving during the schism and the wars of Ladislaus, and founded the Oblates of Tor de' Specchi. She saw her guardian angel constantly. Patroness of motorists.

Forty soldiers of the Twelfth Legion left naked on a frozen lake in Armenia under Licinius, with a warm bath on the shore for any who would renounce Christ. One gave in; a guard, seeing forty crowns descending, stripped and took his place. Basil and Gregory of Nyssa preached on them.

A priest of Muslim Córdoba who wrote the Memorial of the Saints to encourage the Christians who publicly confessed Christ and were executed for it, and was himself beheaded for hiding a young convert from Islam, Leocritia.

Prefect of Rome turned monk, then pope in a city of plague and Lombard siege; he fed Rome from the Church's estates, sent Augustine to convert the English, wrote the Pastoral Rule and the Dialogues, and gave his name to the chant. (Kept on September 3 in the new calendar.)

A relative of the emperor Theodosius who at seven entered a convent in Egypt with her widowed mother and, when the emperor summoned her to marry, asked him instead to give her fortune to the poor and free her slaves. She carried stones from place to place to conquer temptation.

Wife of Henry the Fowler and mother of the emperor Otto the Great, who founded monasteries at Quedlinburg and Nordhausen and gave so freely to the poor that her sons accused her of wasting the treasury. She forgave them and outlived the accusation.

A widow of the French court who under Vincent de Paul founded the Daughters of Charity — sisters whose cloister was 'the streets of the city', their chapel the parish church — the first women religious to nurse in the world without enclosure. Patroness of social workers.

A hermit of Edessa who left his cell to convert a pagan village by patience, and years later, disguised as a soldier, walked into a brothel to rescue his niece Mary, who had fled there in despair; he brought her home and she became a saint. Ephrem the Syrian told the story.

A British boy kidnapped by Irish raiders at sixteen, six years a slave herding sheep, who escaped, became a bishop, and returned to the land of his captivity to convert it. His Confession and his Letter to Coroticus are the oldest documents written in Ireland. He used the shamrock, tradition says, to explain the Trinity.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: Bishop of Jerusalem exiled three times by the Arians. His Catechetical Lectures, given in the church of the Holy Sepulchre to those about to be baptised, are the fullest picture we have of how the fourth-century Church explained the Creed and the sacraments to newcomers.

n: Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: The carpenter of Nazareth, 'a just man', who obeyed four dreams, took the pregnant Mary into his home, carried the child to Egypt and back, and taught him a trade. He never speaks in the Gospels. Patron of the universal Church, of workers and of a happy death.

A shepherd boy who saw Aidan's soul carried to heaven and became a monk at Melrose, prior of Lindisfarne, and a hermit on the Inner Farne with the seals and the eider ducks that still bear his name. His body was carried by the monks for a hundred years from the Vikings until it rested at Durham.

The father of Western monks, who left Rome's schools for a cave at Subiaco, founded Monte Cassino, and wrote the Rule — 'a little rule for beginners' — that ordered Europe's prayer and work for fifteen centuries. Today is the day of his death; July 11 is his feast in the new calendar.

'Little John', a carpenter who built priest-holes in the manor houses of Elizabethan England so cunning that some were found only centuries later. Captured after the Gunpowder Plot, he was tortured to death in the Tower without betraying a single hiding place.

A Spanish law professor made archbishop of Lima while still a layman, who learned Quechua, travelled his diocese of eighteen thousand miles on foot three times, confirmed Rose of Lima and Martin de Porres, and fought the conquistadors for the rights of the Indians.

Daughter of Bridget of Sweden, who followed her mother to Rome, lived with her twenty-five years, and carried her body home to Vadstena, where she became abbess of the Bridgettines. Also today: Oscar Romero, archbishop of San Salvador, shot at the altar in 1980.

Nine months before Christmas: Gabriel comes to a girl in Nazareth, and at her 'Be it done to me according to thy word' the Word becomes flesh. For centuries Lady Day was the first day of the year in England. The Angelus, prayed three times daily, is this scene.

A Frisian pupil of Alcuin who rebuilt the missions the pagan Saxons had burned, refused to hurry his morning prayers when Charlemagne summoned him, and became the first bishop of Münster. Also today: Margaret Clitherow, pressed to death at York in 1586 for hiding priests.

A carpenter who walled himself into a cell on a cliff near Lycopolis for fifty years, speaking to visitors through a window on Saturdays and Sundays; the emperor Theodosius twice sent to ask him the outcome of his wars, and both times he answered rightly. Augustine and Jerome mention him.

A monk of St Gall who was poet, sculptor, painter, architect, metalworker, musician and teacher — 'a man of strength and eloquence, skilled in every art', says the chronicler. Some of the earliest tropes of the Mass are his. Ekkehard says he could have been famous and chose to be a monk.

Two Persian monks who visited Christians condemned by King Shapur II and were arrested for it; the acts of their torture are among the most detailed of the Persian persecution. Also today: Gwynllyw and Gwladys, Welsh king and queen who ended as hermits.

Abbot of St Catherine's on Mount Sinai, named for his Ladder of Divine Ascent — thirty steps from renunciation to love, read aloud in Orthodox monasteries every Lent to this day. He had lived forty years as a hermit before being made abbot.

A Persian deacon imprisoned for preaching, released at the request of the Roman ambassador on condition of silence, who kept preaching and was executed by having reeds driven under his nails. Also today: Guy of Pomposa, the abbot Dante's teacher Peter Damian admired.

Bishop of Grenoble for fifty-two years, who gave Bruno and his six companions the mountain valley of the Chartreuse in 1084 and thereby founded the Carthusians. He begged to resign to become a monk himself; three popes refused.

A Calabrian hermit whose followers, the Minims ('the least'), took a fourth vow of perpetual Lent. Summoned to France to cure Louis XI, he instead prepared the king to die. Legend has him crossing the Strait of Messina on his cloak. Patron of sailors.

An Oxford scholar who ploughed his family's fields to save them from ruin, became chancellor of the university and bishop of Chichester against King Henry III's will, and lived like a poor priest. His prayer 'Day by day, dear Lord, of thee three things I pray' is still sung.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: Archbishop of Seville who converted the Visigothic kings from Arianism, presided over the councils of Toledo, and wrote the Etymologies — an encyclopaedia of all ancient knowledge that was the most-copied book of the early Middle Ages. Proposed as patron of the internet.

A Valencian Dominican who preached the end of the world across Spain, France and Italy for twenty years, followed by crowds of penitents, and worked to end the Great Schism though he had served the Avignon pope. Patron of builders.

A Paris canon called to Denmark to reform a lax monastery, who persevered through poverty and hostility to found Æbelholt abbey. Also today: Notker the Stammerer of St Gall, poet of the sequences, whose hymns are still sung at Mass.

t: Priest, founder of the Christian Brothers
b: A canon of Reims who gave his fortune to the poor and founded the Brothers of the Christian Schools — teaching in French instead of Latin, in classes instead of one by one, with training colleges for teachers. Patron of teachers.

A Picardy peasant paralysed for twenty-two years, who from her bed taught catechism and hid priests during the Terror, was suddenly healed, and founded the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur to teach poor girls. 'How good is the good God!'

A Belgian noblewoman whose parents, husband, sister and four children are all saints; when her husband became a monk she founded the convent around which the city of Mons grew. Also today: Casilda of Toledo, the Moorish princess who fed Christian prisoners.

Bishop and founder of the cathedral school of Chartres, the first great school of the eleventh century; he rebuilt the cathedral after the fire of 1020 and wrote the Easter hymn Chorus novae Jerusalem.

Bishop of Kraków who excommunicated King Boleslaus II for his cruelties and was cut down by the king himself at the altar of St Michael's church. Poland's Thomas Becket; Kraków's cathedral holds his relics beside the Polish kings.

An African-born bishop of Verona whose ninety surviving sermons show a Church fresh from persecution: he baptised the crowd every Easter, insisted that the wealthy share, and is shown with a fish on his crozier. Also today: Julius I, the pope who defended Athanasius.

The last pope venerated as a martyr. Elected without the emperor's consent, he condemned Monothelitism at the Lateran Council; Constans II had him kidnapped, tried in Constantinople, stripped, chained and exiled to the Crimea, where he died of hunger and neglect.

Valerian, the husband of Cecilia, converted by her on their wedding night; Tiburtius his brother; and Maximus the officer who was to execute them and instead joined them. They were buried by Cecilia on the Appian Way.

A noblewoman of Alsace who washed the clothes of the poor of her village with her own hands. Also today: Damien of Molokai (traditional date), the Belgian priest who lived and died among the lepers of Hawaii — 'We lepers.'

The visionary of Lourdes died on this day in 1879 (see February 18). Also today: Benedict Joseph Labre, the French beggar who wandered Europe's shrines in rags for thirteen years, sleeping in the ruins of the Colosseum, and died in Holy Week to the cry of the children of Rome, 'The saint is dead!'

An Englishman who became the third abbot of Cîteaux and saved the dying reform by receiving the young Bernard and his thirty companions in 1112. His Charter of Charity gave the Cistercians their constitution; the Cîteaux Bible he corrected against the Hebrew survives.

A Roman senator denounced as a Christian by his own slave under Commodus; his defence before the Senate, one of the earliest Christian apologies, is preserved. He was beheaded. Also today: Galdinus of Milan, who died in the pulpit preaching against heresy.

An Alsatian bishop who entered Rome barefoot as a pilgrim to be elected, and travelled Europe holding councils against simony and clerical marriage with Hildebrand and Humbert at his side. He died months before his legate's excommunication of the patriarch of Constantinople began the Great Schism.

Made prioress at fifteen by papal dispensation, she founded a Dominican convent in her home town and lived on bread and water. Catherine of Siena visited her incorrupt body and, bending to kiss the foot, saw it lift to meet her.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: Abbot of Bec and archbishop of Canterbury, exiled twice by Norman kings over the freedom of the Church. His Proslogion offers the ontological argument — God as 'that than which nothing greater can be thought' — and Cur Deus Homo asks why God became man. 'Faith seeking understanding.'

Soter (d. 174) was praised by Dionysius of Corinth for the alms Rome sent to poor churches; Caius (d. 296), a Dalmatian, ruled through the calm before Diocletian's storm. Also today: Theodore of Sykeon, the innkeeper's son who became a bishop and a wonder-worker.

A soldier of Cappadocia martyred at Lydda under Diocletian; the dragon came later, from the Golden Legend. Crusaders brought him to England, where he displaced Edward the Confessor as patron. Also today: Adalbert of Prague, apostle of the Prussians, martyred in 997.

A lawyer known as 'the poor man's advocate' who became a Capuchin and was sent to preach to the Calvinists of the Grisons; he was cut down by a mob at Seewis after preaching on 'one Lord, one faith, one baptism'. First martyr of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith.

John Mark of Jerusalem, in whose mother's house the Church met, who turned back on Paul's first journey and later became 'my son' to Peter, whose preaching he set down in the shortest and earliest Gospel. Founder of the Church of Alexandria; his relics were smuggled to Venice in 828 under a load of pork.

A fresco of the Virgin and Child that, tradition says, appeared on a wall at Genazzano near Rome in 1467; the sanctuary became a place of pilgrimage for popes. Also today: Cletus and Marcellinus, early popes.

A servant in the Fatinelli household at Lucca for forty-eight years, who gave her food to the poor and once, legend says, had her baking done by angels while she prayed. Patroness of domestic workers; her body lies incorrupt in San Frediano.

A Marist missionary to the island of Futuna in the Pacific, clubbed to death by the king's warriors when the king's son asked for baptism. Within a year the whole island was Christian. First martyr of Oceania. Also today: Louis de Montfort, apostle of Marian consecration.

t: Virgin and Doctor of the Church, patroness of Europe
b: The twenty-fourth child of a Sienese dyer, a Dominican tertiary who nursed plague victims, dictated the Dialogue in ecstasy, told the pope to his face to return from Avignon to Rome — and he did. She died at thirty-three. The first woman named Doctor of the Church, with Teresa of Ávila.

A Dominican inquisitor who as pope enforced the reforms of Trent, published the Roman Catechism, Breviary and Missal, and organised the Holy League that won at Lepanto — he is said to have known of the victory by vision before the news arrived. He still wore his white Dominican habit; popes have worn white since.

Instituted by Pius XII in 1955 to set the carpenter of Nazareth beside the workers' May Day: the dignity of labour in the hands that taught the Son of God to use a plane. Also today: Peregrine Laziosi, patron of cancer patients, and the prophet Jeremias in the Martyrology.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: Bishop of Alexandria for forty-five years, seventeen of them in five exiles, for insisting against the Arian emperors that the Son is 'of one substance with the Father'. Athanasius contra mundum — 'against the world'. He wrote the Life of Anthony and first listed exactly our twenty-seven New Testament books.

Philip of Bethsaida, who brought Nathanael to Jesus and asked at the Last Supper, 'Lord, show us the Father'; and James the Less, son of Alphaeus. Their relics lie together in the church of the Twelve Apostles in Rome, dedicated on this day.

A Roman officer in Noricum who declared himself a Christian when ordered to persecute them, and was drowned in the Enns with a millstone round his neck. Patron of Austria, Poland and firefighters. Also today: the English Martyrs of the Reformation (England and Wales).

A monk of Lérins made archbishop of Arles at twenty-nine, who worked with his hands to feed the poor and sold the church plate to ransom captives. His quarrel with Pope Leo the Great over the limits of his authority is a landmark in the history of the papacy.

A boy of the oratory at Turin who resolved at his First Communion, 'Death rather than sin', broke up fights with a crucifix, and died at fourteen. Don Bosco wrote his life; Pius XII canonised him in 1954 as the youngest non-martyr saint of his time.

Bishop of Hexham and York who ordained the Venerable Bede, and retired to the monastery he founded at Beverley. Henry V attributed Agincourt, fought on the day of his translation, to his prayers. Also today: Rose Venerini, foundress of the first public schools for girls in Italy.

The archangel's appearance on Monte Gargano in Apulia in 492, where a cave became the oldest Michael shrine in the West; pilgrims and crusaders have climbed to it ever since. Also today: Peter of Tarentaise, the Cistercian archbishop who fled his see to hide as a lay brother.

A pagan conscript in the Egyptian army converted by the kindness of Christians to the prisoners, who founded at Tabennisi the first monastery where monks lived under a common rule — nine monasteries and three thousand monks by his death. Basil and Benedict both built on his rule.

A Flemish farmer's son who volunteered for the leper colony of Kalaupapa on Molokai, built its church, coffins and homes with his own hands, and after sixteen years began a sermon 'We lepers'. He died of the disease at forty-nine. Patron of those with leprosy and HIV. Also today: John of Ávila, Doctor of the Church.

A Sardinian peasant who for forty years begged for his friary through the streets of Cagliari, refusing the alms of a usurer, and was loved by the whole city. Also today: Mamertus of Vienne, who instituted the Rogation days of prayer for the harvest.

Nereus and Achilleus, Praetorian soldiers who threw away their arms, and Pancras, a fourteen-year-old Phrygian orphan beheaded under Diocletian. Augustine of Canterbury dedicated his first church in England to Pancras; the London station keeps the name.

On 13 May 1917 three shepherd children — Lúcia, Francisco and Jacinta — saw a lady 'brighter than the sun' over a holm oak at the Cova da Iria in Portugal, who asked for the Rosary and returned on the thirteenth of each month until October, when seventy thousand saw the sun dance. John Paul II was shot on this day in 1981 and credited her with his life.

After the Ascension the Eleven chose by lot, between Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias, one 'who accompanied us all the time the Lord Jesus came in and went out among us' to take Judas's place. Nothing more is known; tradition sends him to Ethiopia.

A day labourer of Madrid who went to Mass before work every morning; his employer, checking why he was late to the fields, found angels ploughing beside him. He and his wife Maria de la Cabeza shared their food with the poor and the birds. Patron of Madrid and of farmers.

An English Carmelite general to whom, tradition says, the Virgin gave the brown scapular in 1251 at Cambridge. He steered the order from Palestinian hermits to European friars. Also today: Brendan the Navigator, whose legendary voyage may have touched America, and John Nepomucene, drowned in the Vltava.

A Spanish shepherd who taught himself to read to pray the office, became a Franciscan doorkeeper, and adored the Blessed Sacrament for hours at night. Patron of Eucharistic congresses; his tomb at Villareal was desecrated in 1936.

Sent by the Arian king Theodoric to Constantinople to plead for the Arians of the East — the first pope to visit the city — he was received with such honour that Theodoric, suspecting treachery, imprisoned him at Ravenna on his return, where he died of ill-treatment.

Abbot of Glastonbury, adviser to seven kings, and archbishop who restored English monasticism after the Danes. A skilled metalworker and harpist — legend says he seized the devil's nose with his tongs. Also today: Celestine V, the hermit pope who resigned, and Ivo of Kermartin, patron of lawyers.

The greatest preacher of fifteenth-century Italy, who held crowds for hours in the piazzas, ended feuds, burned vanities, and held up the monogram IHS of the Holy Name until it was painted on every city gate. He refused three bishoprics.

Twenty-two priests and three laymen shot during the Cristero War, when the Mexican government closed the churches. Magallanes, a parish priest who had founded a seminary, gave his executioners absolution and his remaining possessions: 'I die innocent, and I ask God that my blood may serve to unite my Mexican brethren.'

Married at twelve to a violent man she reformed by patience, widowed when he was murdered, and bereft of two sons who died before they could avenge him; then an Augustinian nun who bore a thorn-wound from a crucifix for fifteen years. Patroness of impossible causes.

A Roman priest, epileptic, who spent his life among the cattle-drovers of the Campagna, the beggars and the homeless women of Rome, hearing confessions all day. He gave away everything and died in a hospital bed. Also today: Desiderius of Vienne, martyred by Queen Brunhilda.

Instituted by Pius VII in 1815 in thanks for his release from Napoleon's prison; the title comes from the Litany of Loreto after Lepanto. Don Bosco built the great basilica of Turin under it. Also today: David of Scotland, the king who founded Melrose and Holyrood.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: A monk of Jarrow from the age of seven who never travelled beyond Northumbria and wrote the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, the first history of England and the book that popularised dating years from Christ's birth. He died dictating a translation of John's Gospel: 'It is finished.' Also today: Gregory VII and Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi.

The 'Apostle of Rome', a Florentine layman who spent seventeen years praying in the catacombs and talking to anyone, then founded the Oratory where laymen prayed, sang and laughed together; his heart was physically enlarged by a vision at Pentecost. 'Be good, if you can.'

Prior of Gregory the Great's monastery in Rome, sent with forty monks to Kent in 597, so afraid of the English that he turned back once. King Ethelbert met him under an oak, was baptised, and gave him Canterbury. Gregory's letters answering his practical questions are in Bede.

Archdeacon of Aosta who built hospices on the two Alpine passes that bear his name, staffed by canons and their dogs, to rescue pilgrims to Rome from the snow. Patron of mountaineers. Also today: Germanus of Paris, whose abbey became Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

Giovanni Battista Montini, who completed the Second Vatican Council, reformed the liturgy and the calendar, was the first pope to fly, to visit the Holy Land and to address the United Nations, and wrote Humanae Vitae. Also today: Maximinus of Trier, who sheltered Athanasius in exile.

A peasant girl of Domrémy whose voices sent her at seventeen to raise the siege of Orléans and crown Charles VII at Reims; captured by the Burgundians, sold to the English, condemned by a church court and burned at Rouen at nineteen. Her sentence was annulled in 1456 and she was canonised in 1920.

n: The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: Mary hurries to the hill country to her cousin Elizabeth, and John leaps in the womb at her greeting: 'Blessed art thou among women.' Her answer is the Magnificat, sung by the Church every evening since. The feast closes the month of Mary.

A Samaritan philosopher who tried the Stoics, Aristotelians and Pythagoreans before an old man on a beach pointed him to the prophets. He kept his philosopher's cloak, opened a school in Rome, wrote the Apologies describing the Sunday Eucharist to the emperor, and was beheaded with six students.

A priest and an exorcist beheaded in a wood outside Rome under Diocletian so that their graves would not be found; their executioner told the story after becoming a Christian. Constantine built a basilica over them and buried his mother beside it. Named in the Roman Canon.

Twenty-two pages of the court of King Mwanga of Buganda, Catholics and Anglicans, aged thirteen to thirty, who refused the king's demands and were burned alive at Namugongo. Charles, master of the pages, had baptised four of them the night before. Africa's first canonised martyrs.

A Neapolitan noble cured of leprosy who founded the Clerks Regular Minor, vowed not to seek office, and spent nights in adoration: 'Zeal for thy house has eaten me up' was found written over his heart. Also today: Optatus of Milevis, who answered the Donatists.

t: Bishop and martyr, apostle of Germany
b: Winfrid of Devon, who felled the sacred oak of Thor at Geismar before a crowd waiting for the god to strike him, founded Fulda, crowned Pepin, and reformed the Frankish Church. At seventy-nine he went back to the Frisians and was killed at Dokkum, holding a Gospel book over his head.

A worldly courtier thrown from his horse by lightning, who became a wandering preacher, founded the white canons at Prémontré, and as archbishop of Magdeburg fought for the reform of the clergy. Patron of Bohemia; his relics are at Strahov in Prague.

One of the founders of Fountains Abbey and first abbot of Newminster in Northumberland; the hermit Godric saw his soul rise to heaven as a ball of fire. Also today: Colman of Dromore and Meriadoc of Vannes.

Twice archbishop of York, deposed through the intrigues of the Cistercians and restored after Bernard's death; as he re-entered York the Ouse bridge collapsed under the crowd and no one was hurt. He died a month later, perhaps poisoned in the chalice. Also today: Medard, patron of the weather.

t: Deacon and Doctor of the Church
b: 'The harp of the Holy Spirit', a deacon of Nisibis and Edessa who wrote theology as hymns — hundreds of them, sung by choirs of women he trained — and never accepted ordination as a priest. He died nursing the victims of famine. Also today: Columba of Iona.

An English princess raised in Hungary who married Malcolm III of Scotland, reformed the Scottish Church, fed orphans with her own hands every morning, and founded Dunfermline. Her son David is a saint; her chapel is the oldest building in Edinburgh. (November 16 in the new calendar.)

Joseph of Cyprus, 'son of consolation', who sold his field for the apostles, vouched for the converted Saul when everyone feared him, fetched him from Tarsus to Antioch, and shared his first journey — then parted from him over Mark. Tradition says he was stoned at Salamis.

A preacher of Salamanca who reconciled the feuding nobles of the city and was, it is said, poisoned by a woman whose lover he had converted. Also today: Onuphrius, the hairy hermit of the Egyptian desert loved by medieval pilgrims.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: A Portuguese Augustinian who became a Franciscan after seeing the bodies of the first Franciscan martyrs of Morocco, was discovered as a preacher by accident at an ordination, and held Italy and France spellbound; the fish of Rimini listened when the heretics would not. He died at thirty-five. Patron of lost things.

The Roman Martyrology today remembers Eliseus, disciple and successor of Elias, on whom the double portion of his spirit fell. Also today: Methodius of Constantinople, who restored the icons in 843 — the 'Triumph of Orthodoxy'.

A Sicilian boy, his tutor and his nurse, martyred under Diocletian; Vitus became one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, invoked against epilepsy and the dancing mania called St Vitus's dance. Also today: Germaine Cousin, the sickly shepherdess of Pibrac whose apron of bread turned to flowers.

A Jesuit who walked the mountains of the Vivarais in winter preaching to Huguenots and Catholics alike, founded refuges for prostitutes, and died of pneumonia caught on a mission. The Curé of Ars made a pilgrimage to his grave on foot as a seminarian.

A wealthy Pisan musician converted by a hermit, who lived as a beggar in the Holy Land for years and returned to Pisa to a life of prayer and miracles; his tomb is in the cathedral. Also today: Emily de Vialar, foundress of the Sisters of St Joseph of the Apparition.
See June 9. Also today: Mark and Marcellian, twin brothers of Rome martyred under Diocletian, encouraged by Sebastian when their parents begged them to apostatise.

Founder of the Camaldolese (see February 7 in the traditional calendar): a wanderer who founded hermitages across Italy, and wrote for his hermits the Brief Rule — 'Empty yourself completely and sit waiting, content with the grace of God, like the chick who tastes nothing and eats nothing but what his mother brings him.'

Son of Pope Hormisdas, deposed by the general Belisarius at the empress Theodora's command for refusing to restore a Monophysite patriarch, and starved to death on the island of Palmarola. Also today: Alban, the first martyr of Britain (traditional date).

Heir to the marquisate of Castiglione, who renounced it at seventeen to become a Jesuit against his father's fury, and died at twenty-three nursing plague victims in Rome. Patron of youth and of AIDS caregivers.

Fisher, bishop of Rochester, the only English bishop to refuse Henry VIII's supremacy, beheaded on June 22; More, lord chancellor, author of Utopia, beheaded on July 6: 'I die the king's good servant, and God's first.' Also today: Paulinus of Nola, the senator-poet.

A Piedmontese priest, hunchbacked and tireless, who trained the clergy of Turin, was Don Bosco's confessor and benefactor, and accompanied sixty condemned men to the gallows — 'my hanged saints', he called them. Also today: Etheldreda, foundress of Ely.

n: The Nativity of Saint John the Baptist
b: Six months before Christmas, at midsummer, the Church keeps the birthday of the forerunner — the only saint besides the Virgin whose birth is a feast. His father Zachary's tongue is loosed to sing the Benedictus. 'He must increase, but I must decrease': the days shorten from here.

A married layman of Marseilles who defended Augustine's teaching on grace against the monks of Lérins and became secretary to Leo the Great. Also today: William of Vercelli, founder of Montevergine, and Adalbert of Egmond.

Two brothers, officers of the household of Constantine's daughter, martyred in their own house on the Caelian hill under Julian the Apostate; the basilica built over it stands on the excavated rooms. Named in the Roman Canon. Also today: Josemaría Escrivá, founder of Opus Dei.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: Patriarch of Alexandria who fought Nestorius for the title Theotokos and presided at the Council of Ephesus (431) which defined that Mary is the Mother of God, since her child is one person, divine and human. A fierce man; a decisive theologian. Also today: Our Lady of Perpetual Help.

t: Bishop and martyr, Doctor of the Church
b: A pupil of Polycarp who was a pupil of John, bishop of Lyon after the martyrs of 177. His Against Heresies demolished the Gnostics with the rule of faith and the succession of bishops; 'the glory of God is a living man.' Named Doctor of the Church in 2022.

wp: Feast of Saints Peter and Paul
b: The two pillars, martyred at Rome under Nero: Peter crucified head-down on the Vatican hill, Paul beheaded on the Ostian Way. Rome keeps their feast as its own birthday; the pallium is given to new archbishops today. 'Thou art Peter'; 'I have fought the good fight.'

n: The First Martyrs of the Church of Rome
wp: First Martyrs of the Church of Rome
b: The Christians Nero blamed for the fire of 64 and killed in his gardens — sewn into animal skins for the dogs, crucified, or burned as torches to light the night, as Tacitus records. Peter and Paul died in the same persecution.

A Mallorcan Franciscan professor who at fifty walked the length of California founding nine missions from San Diego to San Francisco, baptising six thousand, defending the Indians against the soldiers, and walking on an ulcerated leg the whole way. Also today: Oliver Plunkett, hanged at Tyburn in 1681.

Before 1969 the Visitation was kept today, after the Octave of the Baptist. Also today: Processus and Martinian, the jailers of Peter in the Mamertine prison, converted and martyred; and Otto of Bamberg, apostle of Pomerania.

'Didymus', the twin, who said 'Let us also go, that we may die with him', asked 'Lord, we know not whither thou goest', and refused to believe the Resurrection until he touched the wounds — then made the fullest confession in the Gospels: 'My Lord and my God.' Tradition takes him to India, where the Christians of Kerala still call themselves his.

Great-niece of Elizabeth of Hungary, married at twelve to the faithless King Denis, who raised his illegitimate children, rode between two armies to stop a war between her husband and her son, and died a Franciscan tertiary on another peace mission. Also today: Independence Day (United States).

A physician of Cremona who became a priest and founded the Barnabites, the first clerks regular of the Catholic Reformation, promoting the Forty Hours' devotion and the ringing of bells at three on Friday afternoons. He died at thirty-six.

An eleven-year-old farm girl of the Pontine marshes stabbed fourteen times by a neighbour, Alessandro Serenelli, when she refused him; she forgave him before dying. He repented in prison after a dream of her, and attended her canonisation in 1950 with her mother.

An English monk who made a seven-year pilgrimage to the Holy Land — the earliest English travel narrative, dictated to a nun — and was sent by Boniface, his kinsman, to be first bishop of Eichstätt. Also today: Palladius, first bishop sent to the Irish.

t: Bishop and martyr, apostle of Franconia
b: An Irish missionary bishop killed at Würzburg with two companions for telling Duke Gozbert that his marriage to his brother's widow was unlawful. His skull is carried through Würzburg on his feast. Also today: Aquila and Priscilla, the tentmakers who taught Apollos.

A hundred and twenty martyrs of China, from 1648 to 1930: eighty-seven Chinese and thirty-three missionaries. Zhao Rong was a soldier who escorted a bishop to his execution, was converted by his bearing, became a priest, and was tortured to death in Sichuan. Also today: the Martyrs of Gorkum.

A Roman widow who watched her seven sons executed one by one under Marcus Aurelius and then died herself, encouraging each to look up to heaven. Also today: Knud, king of Denmark, and Rufina and Secunda, virgin martyrs of Rome.

The founder of Western monasticism (see March 21). His Rule balances prayer, work and reading — ora et labora — with a moderation that let it outlast every other. 'Listen, my son, to the precepts of the master, and incline the ear of your heart.' Paul VI named him patron of Europe in 1964.

A Florentine knight who met his brother's murderer unarmed on Good Friday, spared him when he begged in the form of the cross, and saw the crucifix in San Miniato bow to him. He became a monk, founded Vallombrosa and fought simony. Also today: Veronica, who wiped the face of Christ.

Duke of Bavaria and last Ottonian emperor, who founded the bishopric of Bamberg, supported Cluny's reform, and, tradition says, lived in continence with his wife Cunegund; both are saints. He asked to be received as a monk at Verdun and was ordered by the abbot to keep ruling.

A Mohawk girl of the Hudson valley, scarred and half-blinded by smallpox at four, baptised by Jesuits at twenty and driven from her village, who walked two hundred miles to the mission at Kahnawake and died at twenty-four. 'The Lily of the Mohawks', first Native American saint. Also today: Camillus de Lellis.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: The 'Seraphic Doctor', minister general of the Franciscans who wrote the official life of Francis and The Journey of the Mind to God; a cardinal who was found washing dishes when the red hat arrived. He died during the Council of Lyon, where Thomas Aquinas had been travelling to meet him.

The mountain where Elias called down fire, later home of the hermits who became the Carmelites. The brown scapular given to Simon Stock is the devotion's sign; Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross and Thérèse of Lisieux are its children.

Sixteen Carmelite nuns guillotined in Paris ten days before the fall of Robespierre, singing the Veni Creator as they mounted the scaffold one by one, the prioress last. Poulenc's opera Dialogues of the Carmelites tells their story. Also today: Alexis, the man of God, and Leo IV.

A giant of a soldier, gambler and brawler with an incurable leg wound, converted at twenty-five, who founded the Ministers of the Sick to nurse the dying in hospitals and on battlefields — the red cross on their habit preceded the Red Cross by three centuries. (July 14 in the new calendar.)

Eldest sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa, who persuaded Basil to give up his rhetorician's ambition for monastic life, and turned the family estate into a monastery. Gregory's On the Soul and the Resurrection records her deathbed conversation.

By tradition a disciple of Peter sent to Ravenna as its first bishop, exiled and beaten repeatedly, and finally martyred at Classe, where the sixth-century basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe shows him among lambs in a green paradise. Also today: Margaret of Antioch, who burst from the dragon.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: A Capuchin who spoke Hebrew well enough to preach in synagogues, led the imperial army against the Turks at Székesfehérvár armed only with a crucifix, and died on an embassy to Spain on his sixtieth birthday. His collected works fill fifteen volumes.

Freed of seven demons, she followed Jesus from Galilee, stood at the cross, and came to the tomb while it was still dark — the first to see him risen, sent to tell the apostles. Gregory the Great's identification of her with the sinful woman of Luke 7 shaped a thousand paintings but is not in the text. Pope Francis raised the day to a feast in 2016.

A noblewoman and mother of eight who after her husband's death received visions she dictated in Swedish — the Revelations, read all over Europe — founded the Bridgettines at Vadstena, went to Rome to demand the pope's return from Avignon, and died there after a pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

A Lebanese Maronite monk who spent his last twenty-three years in a hermitage at Annaya, silent, eating once a day, and died on Christmas Eve after a stroke at Mass. Lights over his grave, an incorrupt body and a flood of cures made him Lebanon's saint for Christians and Muslims alike.

Son of Zebedee, brother of John, 'son of thunder', present at the Transfiguration and Gethsemani, the first apostle to be martyred — beheaded by Herod Agrippa in 44. Spain claims his body at Compostela, the goal of Europe's great pilgrim road, the Camino.

t: Parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: The grandparents of Jesus, unnamed in Scripture, known from the second-century Protoevangelium of James: an old, childless couple whose prayer was answered with Mary. Anne became the patroness of mothers, grandmothers and Brittany; Luther called on her when the lightning struck.

Physician to the emperor Maximian at Nicomedia, who treated the poor for nothing and was beheaded under Diocletian; his blood at Ravello liquefies on his feast. One of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, patron of doctors. Also today: the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus.

Nazarius and the boy Celsus, martyrs of Milan whose bodies Ambrose discovered in 395; Victor I, the African pope who fixed Easter on a Sunday; and Innocent I, who condemned Pelagius. Also today: Samson of Dol, apostle of Brittany.

The family of Bethany where Jesus was at home. Martha, 'busy about much serving', who confessed 'Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God' before her brother was raised; Mary, who chose the better part; Lazarus, four days dead. Pope Francis joined the three in one memorial in 2021.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: 'Golden-worded' bishop of Ravenna when it was the imperial capital, whose short, vivid sermons — he feared boring his congregation — survive by the hundred. He told Eutyches to submit to the pope, 'since blessed Peter lives and presides in his own see.' Also today: Abdon and Sennen, Persian martyrs.

A Basque courtier whose leg was shattered by a cannonball at Pamplona; reading the lives of Christ and the saints in convalescence, he hung up his sword at Montserrat, wrote the Spiritual Exercises in a cave at Manresa, studied at Paris at thirty-three, and founded the Society of Jesus. 'For the greater glory of God.'

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: A Neapolitan lawyer who lost a case through his own error and left the bar for the priesthood, founded the Redemptorists to preach to the abandoned peasants of the hills, and wrote the Moral Theology that made confession gentler. He composed Christmas carols still sung in Italy. Patron of confessors.

A Sardinian, first bishop of Vercelli, who lived with his clergy as monks, refused at Milan to condemn Athanasius, and was exiled to Palestine and Egypt by Constantius. Also today: Peter Julian Eymard, apostle of the Eucharist, and Our Lady of the Angels (the Portiuncula).

The seller of purple at Philippi 'whose heart the Lord opened' to hear Paul by the river; she and her household were baptised, and she insisted the apostles lodge with her — the first Christian in Europe. Also today: Nicodemus, and the Finding of the relics of Stephen.

A farm boy who could barely learn Latin, sent to the village of Ars because 'there is not much love of God there', where for forty years he heard confessions up to sixteen hours a day, fought the devil at night, and drew a hundred thousand pilgrims a year. Patron of parish priests.

n: The Dedication of Saint Mary Major
b: The first church in the West dedicated to Mary, built by Pope Sixtus III after the Council of Ephesus (431). Legend tells of snow falling on the Esquiline in August to mark the site — 'Our Lady of the Snows'; white petals fall from the ceiling at Mass today. It houses the relics of the manger.

On the mountain Jesus' face shines like the sun, Moses and Elias speak with him, and the voice from the cloud says 'This is my beloved Son.' The Eastern Church's great August feast; the West adopted it in 1457 to mark the victory over the Turks at Belgrade. Hiroshima was bombed on this day in 1945.

Sixtus, seized while celebrating Mass in the catacomb of Callistus and beheaded in his chair under Valerian, four days before his deacon Lawrence; named in the Roman Canon. Cajetan (d. 1547), founder of the Theatines, who set up pawnshops that charged no interest for the poor of Naples.

t: Priest, founder of the Order of Preachers
b: A Castilian canon who sold his books to feed the starving, met the Albigensian heretics in Languedoc and saw that only poor, learned preachers could answer them, and founded the Dominicans — 'to praise, to bless, to preach'. Tradition gives him the Rosary. He spoke only to God or of God.

t: Virgin and martyr, patroness of Europe
b: Edith Stein, a Jewish philosopher, pupil of Husserl and atheist, who read Teresa of Ávila's autobiography in one night and said 'this is the truth'; baptised in 1922, a Carmelite in 1933, she was taken from her Dutch convent by the Gestapo and gassed at Auschwitz with her sister Rosa.

Archdeacon of Rome, ordered to hand over the Church's treasures, who presented the poor of the city: 'These are the treasures of the Church.' Roasted on a gridiron, he is said to have told his executioners, 'Turn me over, this side is done.' Rome's most loved martyr after Peter and Paul; the August meteors are his tears.

t: Virgin, foundress of the Poor Clares
b: A noble girl of eighteen who slipped out of her father's house on Palm Sunday night to have her hair cut by Francis at the Portiuncula, and for forty-two years at San Damiano fought popes to keep the 'privilege of poverty'. She drove the Saracens from Assisi's walls holding the Blessed Sacrament. Patroness of television.

A widow with four children who, under the direction of Francis de Sales, founded the Visitation nuns for women too frail for the great austerities; eighty-seven convents by her death. Her grandson was the father of Madame de Sévigné. Also today: Euplius, the deacon of Catania who carried the Gospels to his death.

Hippolytus, the learned priest who set himself up as the first antipope, and Pontian, the lawful pope, were deported together to the mines of Sardinia under Maximinus, reconciled there, and died. Hippolytus's Apostolic Tradition preserves the oldest Eucharistic Prayer still in use.

A Polish Franciscan who founded the City of the Immaculate, the largest friary in the world, and a mission in Nagasaki. At Auschwitz, when a prisoner with a family was chosen for the starvation bunker, he stepped forward: 'I am a Catholic priest; I wish to take his place.' He led the dying in hymns for two weeks and was killed by injection.

n: The Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: At the end of her life Mary was taken body and soul into heaven — believed since the earliest centuries (the East calls it the Dormition), defined by Pius XII in 1950. 'A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet' (Rev 12). Harvests and herbs are blessed today across Europe.

The Magyar prince Vajk, baptised at ten, crowned with a crown sent by the pope in the year 1000, who made Hungary a Christian kingdom with ten bishoprics, laws against pagan practice, and open hands to the poor. His right hand is carried through Budapest on his feast. Also today: Roch, invoked against plague.

A canon of Kraków who received the habit from Dominic himself in Rome and preached from the Baltic to Kiev; fleeing the Tatars, he carried the Blessed Sacrament and a heavy statue of Mary across the Dnieper. 'The Apostle of the North.' Also today: Clare of Montefalco.

An innkeeper's daughter who became the mother of Constantine, and at nearly eighty went to Jerusalem, where she built the churches of the Nativity and the Ascension and, tradition says, found the True Cross. Also today: Agapitus of Palestrina, a boy martyr, and Alberto Hurtado of Chile.

A Norman missionary who preached a hundred parish missions, nursed plague victims in a barrel so as not to infect his community, founded the Eudists to train priests and the Sisters of Our Lady of Charity for penitent women, and first composed a Mass of the Sacred Heart (1672).

t: Abbot and Doctor of the Church
b: A Burgundian noble who entered Cîteaux at twenty-one with thirty relatives and friends, founded Clairvaux and sixty-eight daughter houses, ended a papal schism, preached the Second Crusade, fought Abelard, and wrote of the love of God with such sweetness that he is called the 'mellifluous doctor'. Dante makes him the guide to the Virgin.

Giuseppe Sarto, a village postman's son, who as pope lowered the age of First Communion to seven, urged daily Communion, reformed the Breviary and church music (Gregorian chant restored), codified canon law, and fought Modernism. He died a fortnight after the outbreak of the First World War, of grief, they said.

n: The Queenship of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: The octave of the Assumption: Mary crowned as queen beside her Son — 'the queen stood on thy right hand in gilded clothing' (Ps 44). Pius XII instituted the feast in 1954; the fifth Glorious Mystery of the Rosary is this scene.

Isabel Flores, a beauty of Lima who rubbed pepper on her face to spoil it, took the Dominican habit as a tertiary, lived in a hut in her parents' garden, and cared for the sick Indians and slaves of the city. She died at thirty-one. First saint of the Americas, patroness of Peru and the Philippines.

Usually identified with Nathanael, 'an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile', who asked whether anything good could come from Nazareth. Tradition sends him to Armenia, where he was flayed alive — Michelangelo painted his own face on the skin Bartholomew holds in the Last Judgement.

The saint-king who fed the poor at his own table, built the Sainte-Chapelle for the Crown of Thorns, judged under the oak of Vincennes, went twice on crusade and died of dysentery at Tunis. Also today: Joseph Calasanz, founder of the Piarists, the first free schools for the poor in Europe.

Pope for eighteen years during which the Roman Church argued over the Trinity; his deacon Callistus guided him. Also today: Teresa of Jesus Jornet, foundress of the Little Sisters of the Abandoned Aged, and Our Lady of Częstochowa, the Black Madonna of Poland.

A North African wife of a pagan with a violent temper, who wept and prayed for seventeen years for her brilliant, wayward son, followed him to Rome and Milan, and saw him baptised by Ambrose. She died at Ostia on the way home, after the shared vision Augustine describes in the Confessions: 'Bury my body anywhere; only remember me at the altar.'

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: The rhetorician of Thagaste who kept a mistress, joined the Manichees, heard Ambrose, and in a Milan garden heard a child sing 'take up and read'; then bishop of Hippo for thirty-five years, author of the Confessions and the City of God, the most influential Christian thinker after Paul. 'Our heart is restless until it rests in thee.'

n: The Passion of Saint John the Baptist
b: Herod Antipas, bound by an oath to a dancing girl, had the Baptist beheaded in the fortress of Machaerus and the head brought in on a dish. 'He must increase, but I must decrease' — the forerunner goes before Christ in death as in birth.

n: Margaret Ward, Anne Line and Margaret Clitherow
b: Margaret Ward, hanged at Tyburn for smuggling a rope to a priest in the Bridewell; Anne Line, hanged in 1601 for harbouring priests; Margaret Clitherow, the butcher's wife of York pressed to death under a door. The three women among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales. Also today: Felix and Adauctus.

An Irish monk of Iona sent to King Oswald, who translated his sermons himself; he walked everywhere, gave away the king's horse to a beggar, ransomed slaves and made them priests, and founded Lindisfarne. Bede loved him above all the saints of the North. Also today: Raymond Nonnatus, ransomer of captives.

A Greek hermit of the Rhône delta whose hind, wounded by the king's hunting arrow, fled to his cave; he founded the abbey of Saint-Gilles, a great stop on the road to Compostela. One of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, patron of cripples and beggars; a hundred and sixty English churches bear his name.

A hundred and ninety-one bishops, priests and religious murdered in the Paris prisons of the Carmes, Saint-Firmin and the Abbaye on 2–3 September 1792 for refusing the oath to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Also today: Stephen of Hungary (traditional date) and William of Roskilde.

t: Pope and Doctor of the Church
b: Prefect of Rome who sold his estates for monasteries, was dragged from his cloister to be pope in a plague year, fed the city, faced the Lombards, sent Augustine to England, wrote the Pastoral Rule for every bishop since, and called himself 'servant of the servants of God'. The chant bears his name.

A Norman noblewoman who lived as a hermit in a cave on Monte Pellegrino; when her bones were found in 1624 and carried through Palermo, the plague ceased. Also today: Moses the Lawgiver in the Roman Martyrology, and Rose of Viterbo.

t: Virgin, foundress of the Missionaries of Charity
b: Anjezë Bojaxhiu of Skopje, a Loreto nun teaching in Calcutta who on a train to Darjeeling heard 'the call within the call' to serve the poorest of the poor; she picked the dying off the streets, and her sisters now work in a hundred and thirty countries. Nobel Peace Prize 1979. Her diaries revealed fifty years of spiritual darkness borne in faith.

An Irish princess who fled a Viking marriage across the sea to Cumbria and founded St Bees; oaths were sworn on her bracelet for centuries. Also today: Zachary the prophet, father of the Baptist, in the Martyrology, and Eleutherius, abbot of Spoleto.

Grandson of Clovis, whose two brothers were murdered by their uncles; he cut off his own royal hair and became a hermit, then a priest, founding the monastery at Saint-Cloud near Paris. Also today: Regina of Autun, virgin martyr, and Melchior Grodziecki and Stephen Pongracz, Jesuit martyrs of Košice.

n: The Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: Nine months after the Immaculate Conception, the Church keeps Mary's birthday — one of only three birthdays in the calendar, with Christ's and the Baptist's. Kept since the sixth century in Jerusalem, at the church built where the house of Joachim and Anne was believed to stand.

A Catalan Jesuit who for forty years met every slave ship arriving at Cartagena, boarding with food, medicine and interpreters, baptising three hundred thousand and calling himself 'the slave of the slaves for ever'. He spent his last four years paralysed and neglected in his room.

An Augustinian friar of the Marches who preached daily for thirty years, visited the slums and prisons, and had a devotion to the souls in purgatory; the bread blessed in his name is given to the sick. Also today: Ambrose Barlow, Benedictine martyr of Lancashire.

Two brothers, servants of Eugenia, beheaded under Valerian; the tomb of Hyacinth was found untouched in the catacomb of Bassilla in 1845, the bones charred, with his name intact. Also today: Paphnutius the bishop, who bore the marks of Diocletian's persecution to the Council of Nicaea.

n: The Most Holy Name of Mary
b: Extended to the whole Church by Innocent XI after the relief of Vienna from the Turks on 12 September 1683 by John Sobieski, who had commended his army to Mary. Also today: Guy of Anderlecht, the poor man's saint of Brussels.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: 'Golden-mouthed', the greatest preacher of the Greek Church, a hermit turned priest of Antioch, dragged to Constantinople as patriarch, where he sold the palace plate for the poor, denounced the empress's vanity, and was exiled twice, dying on a forced march in Pontus: 'Glory be to God for all things.' The Byzantine liturgy bears his name.

n: The Exaltation of the Holy Cross
b: The dedication of Constantine's church of the Holy Sepulchre in 335, when the Cross found by Helena was lifted up for the people to see; and the recovery of the relic from the Persians by Heraclius in 629. 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up.'

The day after the Cross: Mary standing beneath it, 'and thy own soul a sword shall pierce.' The Seven Sorrows — Simeon's prophecy, the flight into Egypt, the loss in the Temple, the way of the cross, the crucifixion, the deposition, the burial — are the Servites' devotion; the Stabat Mater is the day's hymn.

Cornelius, the pope who readmitted the lapsed after penance against the rigorist Novatian, exiled and killed in 253; Cyprian, the rich rhetorician-bishop of Carthage who supported him, wrote On the Unity of the Church, and was beheaded in 258 after a trial whose record survives: 'Thanks be to God.' Both are named in the Roman Canon.

Bellarmine, the Jesuit cardinal of the Counter-Reformation controversies and Galileo's judge, who gave his money to the poor and slept on a straw mattress. Hildegard (d. 1179), the Rhineland abbess whose visions, music, medicine and letters to emperors made her the most remarkable woman of her century; Doctor of the Church since 2012.

A dull, absent-minded boy who was refused by the Capuchins and made a stable hand by the Conventuals, ordained by a lucky examination, and then spent thirty-five years being hidden by his superiors because he rose into the air at Mass, at the name of Mary, at the sight of a lamb. Patron of pilots and of examinees.

Bishop of Benevento beheaded at Pozzuoli under Diocletian. In Naples cathedral a vial of his dried blood liquefies three times a year, usually today, before a crowd that watches for the omen; the years it fails have brought Vesuvius, cholera and war. Also today: Theodore of Canterbury.

n: Andrew Kim Tae-gŏn, Paul Chŏng Ha-sang and Companions
b: A hundred and three martyrs of a Church that Koreans founded themselves from books, without a missionary, in 1784. Andrew Kim, the first Korean priest, beheaded at twenty-five on the Han river; Paul Chŏng, a lay catechist; and women, children and old men, killed in the persecutions of 1839, 1846 and 1866.

Levi the tax collector, called from his customs booth at Capharnaum — 'and he rose up, and followed him' — who gave a dinner for Jesus and his fellow publicans. The first Gospel bears his name, written for Jews to show Jesus as the Messiah of the prophets. Tradition sends him to Ethiopia.

An Egyptian legion of Christians in the Roman army who refused to sacrifice — or, in another telling, to slaughter innocent Christians — at Agaunum in the Alps and were decimated twice and then massacred. The abbey of Saint-Maurice has kept the office in their memory without interruption since 515.

A Capuchin of the Gargano who bore the stigmata for fifty years, heard confessions for hours a day and read hearts, built the Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza hospital, and was suspended for years by a suspicious Vatican. His Mass at San Giovanni Rotondo drew millions. Also today: Linus, second pope.

The feast of the Mercedarians, founded in 1218 by Peter Nolasco to ransom Christian captives from the Moors, its members vowing to take a captive's place if needed. Also today: Gerard of Csanád, the Venetian bishop martyred by pagan Magyars — Budapest's Gellért hill is his.

A hermit of the forests north of Moscow who founded the Trinity Lavra, the mother house of Russian monasticism, and blessed Prince Dmitri before the battle of Kulikovo that broke the Tatar yoke. Russia's most loved saint. Also today: Finbarr of Cork, and Cleophas of Emmaus in the Martyrology.

Twin brothers, physicians of Cilicia who took no fees — the 'unmercenary healers' — beheaded under Diocletian. Justinian rebuilt their church; the Medici took them as patrons; they are named in the Roman Canon. Patrons of doctors, surgeons and pharmacists.

A Gascon peasant's son, tutor in the house of the general of the galleys, who found God among the galley slaves and the country poor, founded the Congregation of the Mission, the Ladies of Charity and, with Louise de Marillac, the Daughters of Charity, and organised the relief of Lorraine in the Thirty Years' War. Patron of all charitable works.

'Good King Wenceslas', duke of Bohemia, raised by his grandmother Ludmila, who built churches and gave to the poor, and was murdered at the church door by his brother Boleslav. Lawrence Ruiz (d. 1637), a Filipino clerk and father of three, tortured to death at Nagasaki: 'Had I a thousand lives, I would offer them all.'

The three angels named in Scripture: Michael, 'who is like God?', captain of the heavenly host against the dragon; Gabriel, who announced the Baptist and the Christ; Raphael, 'God heals', the companion of Tobias. Michaelmas, once a quarter day of the English year.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: The scholar of Stridon who learned Hebrew from a rabbi, dreamed that Christ called him a Ciceronian rather than a Christian, served Pope Damasus, and in a cave at Bethlehem translated the whole Bible into the Latin of this app — the Vulgate, the Bible of the West for a thousand years. Irascible, brilliant, penitent; painted with a lion and a skull. 'Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.'

t: Virgin and Doctor of the Church
b: A Norman girl who entered Carmel at fifteen by begging the pope in person, lived nine hidden years there, and died of tuberculosis at twenty-four. Her autobiography, Story of a Soul, taught the 'little way' of doing small things with great love; Pius XI called her 'the greatest saint of modern times'. Patroness of missions, having never left her convent.

'See that you despise not one of these little ones: for I say to you, that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father' (Matt 18:10). The belief that each soul has an angel to guard it is as old as Psalm 90; the feast became universal under Paul V in 1608.

Duke of Gandía and great-grandson of Pope Alexander VI, who saw the decayed corpse of the empress Isabella and resolved 'never again to serve a master who could die'; widowed, he became a Jesuit and the order's third general. Also today: Gerard of Brogne, the Belgian monastic reformer.

The merchant's son who stripped naked before the bishop to return his father's clothes, rebuilt San Damiano with his hands, kissed a leper, preached to birds, went to the Sultan in the middle of a crusade, built the first Christmas crib at Greccio, received the stigmata on La Verna, and died singing the Canticle of the Sun. Patron of Italy and of ecology.
