A Polish cook and doorkeeper of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy whose diary records Christ asking for the image 'Jesus, I trust in Thee', the chaplet, and a feast of Mercy on the Sunday after Easter — all granted by John Paul II sixty years after her death at thirty-three. Also today: Placid, Benedict's disciple.

Master of the cathedral school of Reims who refused an archbishopric and, with six companions, went to the desert of the Chartreuse in 1084 to found the strictest order in the Church — hermits in a community, silent, never reformed 'because never deformed'. He died in Calabria, where Pope Urban II, his old pupil, had summoned him.

Instituted by Pius V as Our Lady of Victory after the fleet of the Holy League destroyed the Ottoman navy at Lepanto on 7 October 1571, while the confraternities of Rome prayed the Rosary. October is the month of the Rosary; the twenty mysteries are the Gospel told on beads.
See July 23. Also today: Pelagia the Penitent, the actress of Antioch converted by a sermon who lived disguised as a monk on the Mount of Olives; and Thaïs, the courtesan converted by Paphnutius.

n: Denis and Companions; John Henry Newman
b: Denis, first bishop of Paris, beheaded on Montmartre about 250 and said to have carried his head to the site of Saint-Denis; patron of France. Newman (d. 1890), the Oxford leader of the Tractarians who was received into the Catholic Church in 1845, founded the English Oratory, wrote the Apologia and The Dream of Gerontius, and was canonised in 2019.

n: Francis Borgia (traditional date); Daniel and Companions
b: Also today: Daniel and six Franciscans beheaded at Ceuta in 1227 for preaching to Muslims, and Paulinus of York, who baptised the Northumbrians in the Swale.

Angelo Roncalli, a Bergamo farmer's son, nuncio who saved Jews in Turkey, patriarch of Venice, elected at seventy-seven as a caretaker — who called the Second Vatican Council, opened on this day in 1962, and wrote Pacem in Terris. 'Good Pope John.' Also today, in the traditional calendar: the Maternity of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

The Northumbrian who won the Synod of Whitby (664) for the Roman Easter, built stone churches at Ripon and Hexham, was shipwrecked among the pagan South Saxons and converted them, and appealed to Rome against his kings — the first Englishman to do so. Also today: Our Lady of the Pillar, Saragossa.

The last Anglo-Saxon king of the old line, pious, childless, who built Westminster Abbey and was buried there a week after its consecration; his death opened the year of the Norman Conquest. Patron of England until St George. Today is the day of his translation in 1163.

A slave who lost his master's money, was sentenced to the mines of Sardinia, freed, and became deacon in charge of the Christian cemetery on the Appian Way that bears his name — the catacomb of Callistus — then pope. He readmitted repentant sinners and married slaves to free women, to Hippolytus's fury. Killed in a riot.

t: Virgin and Doctor of the Church
b: A Carmelite nun who after twenty lukewarm years was transfixed by an angel's dart, reformed her order barefoot, founded seventeen convents while travelling by mule cart, and wrote the Life, the Way of Perfection and the Interior Castle. 'Let nothing disturb thee.' The first woman Doctor of the Church.

Margaret Mary, the Visitation nun of Paray-le-Monial to whom Christ showed his Heart 'which has so loved men' and asked for the feast of the Sacred Heart and the First Fridays. Hedwig (d. 1243), duchess of Silesia, who walked barefoot in winter and founded the abbey of Trebnitz. Also today: Gerard Majella, patron of expectant mothers.

Third bishop of Antioch, taken in chains to Rome under Trajan, who wrote seven letters on the road begging the Roman Christians not to save him: 'I am the wheat of God, and I shall be ground by the teeth of the beasts to be found the pure bread of Christ.' The first writer to call the Church 'catholic'.

'The beloved physician', Paul's companion in the 'we' passages of Acts, the only Gentile author in the New Testament, who wrote the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles — a quarter of the New Testament — and gave us the Annunciation, the Magnificat, the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son. Tradition makes him the first painter of the Virgin.

n: John de Brébeuf, Isaac Jogues and Companions
b: Eight French Jesuits and lay helpers killed by the Iroquois between 1642 and 1649 in the Huron missions of Canada and New York. Jogues, mutilated and enslaved, returned to France, then went back to the Mohawks who killed him; Brébeuf was tortured for hours at Saint-Ignace and did not cry out. Also today: Paul of the Cross, founder of the Passionists.

A Genoese who saw the black habit with the white heart in a vision and founded the Passionists to keep the memory of Christ's Passion alive by preaching missions; he lived to eighty-one on a hillside on Monte Argentario. Also today: Bertilla Boscardin, the nurse of Treviso.

The founder of monasticism in Palestine, a disciple of Anthony, who lived on the sand dunes near Gaza for decades and fled the crowds his miracles drew — to Egypt, Sicily, Dalmatia and Cyprus, where he died. Jerome wrote his life. Also today: Ursula and her companions, the virgin martyrs of Cologne.

Karol Wojtyła of Kraków, actor, quarryman under the Nazis, philosopher, the first non-Italian pope in 455 years, who visited a hundred and twenty-nine countries, helped bring down Communism in Poland, survived assassination, wrote fourteen encyclicals, and taught the world how to die. Today is the anniversary of his inauguration in 1978.

A lawyer and governor of Perugia imprisoned in a war, who became a Franciscan at thirty, preached across Europe with Bernardine, and at seventy led a peasant army to relieve Belgrade from the Turks in 1456 — the noon Angelus bells commemorate the victory. He died of plague in the camp.

A Catalan weaver who became a missionary preacher of ten thousand sermons, founded the Claretians, was archbishop of Santiago de Cuba (fifteen attempts on his life), confessor to Queen Isabella II, and died in exile in a Cistercian abbey in France. Also today: Raphael the Archangel (traditional calendar).

Two brothers of noble Roman family who fled to Soissons, preached by day and made shoes by night for the poor, and were beheaded under Maximian. Patrons of cobblers; Agincourt was fought on their day, whence Shakespeare's 'we few, we happy few'. Also today: the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.

Fifth pope, a Greek of Jewish descent, who according to the Liber Pontificalis divided Rome into parishes and ordained seven deacons; martyrdom is traditional but unrecorded. Also today: Cedd, bishop of the East Saxons, and Alfred the Great in some English calendars.

A Syrian boy shipwrecked on the Red Sea coast and enslaved at the court of Axum, who rose to be the king's tutor and treasurer, gathered the Christian merchants, went to Athanasius at Alexandria and came back as Ethiopia's first bishop. The Ethiopians call him Abba Salama, 'father of peace'.

Simon 'the Zealot' and Jude 'Thaddeus', who asked at the Last Supper 'Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself to us, and not to the world?' Tradition sends them together to Persia, where they were martyred. Jude, author of the short epistle, became — perhaps through confusion with Judas — the patron of hopeless causes.

Bishop of Jerusalem at nearly a hundred, who turned water to oil for the Easter lamps, was slandered by three men, withdrew to the desert, returned when they died confessing, and lived to a hundred and sixteen. Also today: the Chinese martyrs of 1900 in some calendars.

A widowed wool merchant of Segovia who buried his wife and children, joined the Jesuits at forty as a lay brother, and kept the door of the college in Majorca for forty-six years, greeting each visitor as Christ. Peter Claver was his pupil; Gerard Manley Hopkins wrote his sonnet.

A Swabian monk and missionary to the Magyars, bishop of Regensburg, tutor of the emperor Henry II, who reformed his monasteries and once fled his see to live as a hermit on the Abersee — now the Wolfgangsee. One of the three great German saints of the tenth century. Also today: Alphonsus Rodríguez (new calendar), and All Hallows' Eve.

'A great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations and tribes and peoples and tongues, standing before the throne' (Rev 7:9) — every saint, known and unknown. The feast grew from the dedication of the Pantheon in Rome to Mary and all martyrs in 609. A holy day of obligation.

t: Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed
b: The day for the dead, begun by Odilo of Cluny in 998 and spread to the whole Church: prayer, Masses and cemetery visits for those still being purified, 'for it is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead' (2 Macc 12:46). Priests may say three Masses today. The Dies irae was written for it.

The illegitimate son of a Spanish knight and a freed Black slave of Lima, apprenticed to a barber-surgeon, who joined the Dominicans as a servant, nursed anyone who came — men, dogs, rats — and was seen by witnesses in two places at once. Patron of racial harmony and barbers. Also today: Hubert, patron of hunters.

Nephew of Pius IV, a cardinal at twenty-two who drove the Council of Trent to its conclusion and then, as archbishop of Milan, made it real: seminaries, catechism classes, visitations, and personal service in the plague of 1576 when the governor fled. Shot at by a friar of an order he had reformed, and unhurt.

The priest struck dumb for doubting the angel in the Temple, and the barren kinswoman of Mary who cried, 'Blessed art thou among women.' The Benedictus, Zachary's song, closes every Morning Prayer. Also today: Bertilla of Chelles and the martyrs of Caesarea.

A Frankish courtier converted by Remigius, who refused a bishopric and founded a monastery in the forest of Limousin, where prisoners he freed hung their chains on the church walls. Crusaders spread his cult; patron of prisoners. Also today: Illtud, the Welsh teacher of David and Samson.

A Northumbrian monk trained in Ireland, sent with eleven companions to the pagan Frisians in 690, made archbishop of Utrecht by the pope, who founded Echternach in Luxembourg, where a dancing procession is held to his tomb every Whit Tuesday. Also today: Ernest, abbot of Zwiefalten, martyred at Mecca.

Four Pannonian stonemasons — Claudius, Nicostratus, Simpronian and Castorius — executed for refusing to carve a statue of Aesculapius for Diocletian; patrons of stonemasons and, later, of Freemasons' lodges. Also today: Godfrey of Amiens and the blessed John Duns Scotus.

n: The Dedication of the Lateran Basilica
b: 'The mother and head of all the churches of the city and the world': the cathedral of Rome, given to the Church by Constantine in 324 on the site of the Lateran palace, where every pope until 1309 lived. The feast is kept everywhere as a sign of unity with the See of Peter.

t: Pope and Doctor of the Church
b: The pope who met Attila the Hun at the Mincio in 452 and turned him back from Rome, and whose Tome — 'Peter has spoken through Leo,' the bishops cried — settled the Council of Chalcedon's definition of Christ in two natures. His sermons on the Christmas mystery are read at Matins still.

A Roman cavalry officer who cut his cloak in half for a beggar at Amiens and dreamed of Christ wearing it; a monk under Hilary, then bishop of Tours by acclamation, he founded Marmoutier and evangelised the Gallic countryside. The first non-martyr to be venerated as a saint in the West; four thousand French churches bear his name. Armistice Day.

A Ruthenian archbishop of Polotsk who worked for the union of the Orthodox of Ukraine and Belarus with Rome, and was hacked to death by a mob at Vitebsk. The first Eastern-rite saint canonised by Rome; his body lies in St Peter's.

A frail Lombard schoolteacher who wanted to go to China and was sent by Leo XIII 'not to the East but to the West' — to the Italian immigrants of New York. She crossed the Atlantic thirty times and founded sixty-seven hospitals, schools and orphanages. First United States citizen to be canonised; patroness of immigrants.

A hostage at ten, abbot of Glendalough at twenty-five, archbishop of Dublin through the Norman invasion, who fed the starving, negotiated with Strongbow and Henry II, and died at Eu in Normandy on an embassy for the Irish king. Also today: Nicholas Tavelić, Franciscan martyr of Jerusalem.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: The Swabian Dominican who taught Thomas Aquinas at Cologne and defended him after his death; 'the Universal Doctor', who wrote on every science from botany to astronomy, dissected animals, and made Aristotle safe for the Church. Patron of scientists.

n: Margaret of Scotland; Gertrude the Great
b: Margaret (see June 10). Gertrude (d. 1302), the Benedictine mystic of Helfta whose Herald of Divine Love records her visions of the Sacred Heart three centuries before Paray-le-Monial — the only woman saint called 'the Great'.

A Hungarian princess married at fourteen to the Landgrave of Thuringia, who built a hospital under the Wartburg and fed nine hundred a day; widowed at twenty, driven out by her in-laws, she became a Franciscan tertiary at Marburg and died at twenty-four. The roses in her apron are her sign.

n: The Dedication of the Basilicas of Peter and Paul
b: Constantine's basilica over the tomb of Peter on the Vatican hill and the one over Paul's on the Ostian Way; the present St Peter's was consecrated on this day in 1626. Also today: Rose Philippine Duchesne, the French nun who came to Missouri at forty-nine — 'the woman who always prays', the Potawatomi called her.

Choir mistress of Helfta, 'the nightingale of God', whose Book of Special Grace was recorded by Gertrude; Dante's Matelda in the Earthly Paradise may be her. Also today: Elizabeth of Hungary (traditional date) and Pontian, pope and martyr.

The young king of the East Angles captured by the Great Heathen Army of the Danes, tied to a tree, shot full of arrows and beheaded for refusing to renounce Christ; a wolf guarded the head. Bury St Edmunds grew round his shrine; he was England's patron before George. Also today: Felix of Valois.

n: The Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: Mary as a child brought by Joachim and Anne to the Temple, as the Protoevangelium tells, to be reared among the virgins; the Eastern feast came West in the fourteenth century. Also the day of the dedication in 543 of the New Church of Mary in Jerusalem, and Pro Orantibus day for cloistered religious.

A Roman noblewoman who converted her husband Valerian and his brother, was sentenced to suffocation in her bath and, surviving, struck three times with the sword and left to die over three days. 'While the instruments played, she sang in her heart to God alone' — whence her patronage of music. Maderno's marble shows her as found in 1599, incorrupt.

Clement, the third successor of Peter, whose letter to Corinth (c. 96) is the earliest Christian writing outside the New Testament; tradition has him drowned with an anchor in the Crimea. Columban (d. 615), the Irish monk who founded Luxeuil and Bobbio and rebuked kings and popes with equal freedom. Also today: Miguel Pro, the Mexican Jesuit shot in 1927 crying 'Viva Cristo Rey!'

A hundred and seventeen martyrs of Vietnam from 1745 to 1862 — ninety-six Vietnamese and twenty-one European missionaries, bishops, priests, catechists, mothers and fishermen — beheaded, strangled or hacked to pieces in the persecutions of the Nguyễn emperors. Andrew Dũng-Lạc was a parish priest beheaded at Hanoi.

A learned virgin of Alexandria who, legend says, refuted fifty pagan philosophers before the emperor Maxentius and was condemned to a spiked wheel that shattered at her touch, then beheaded; angels carried her to Sinai, where the monastery bears her name. One of Joan of Arc's voices; patroness of philosophers. Restored to the calendar in 2002.

The greatest Italian mission preacher of the eighteenth century, who spread the Stations of the Cross — he set up five hundred and seventy-one, including one in the Colosseum — and preached the last mission of his life in Rome at seventy-five. Patron of parish missions. Also today: Sylvester Gozzolini, founder of the Sylvestrines.

n: Our Lady of the Miraculous Medal
b: On 27 November 1830 Catherine Labouré, a novice of the Daughters of Charity in the rue du Bac, Paris, saw the Virgin standing on a globe with rays from her hands and the words 'O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee'. The medal struck from it spread through the world within years.

The visionary of the Miraculous Medal, who told only her confessor and spent the next forty-six years as an unknown sister tending the old men of the hospice at Enghien; her identity was revealed months before her death. Her body lies incorrupt in the rue du Bac. Also today: James of the Marches.

First bishop of Toulouse, who passed the Capitol temple daily and was blamed when its oracles fell silent; the pagans tied him to a bull that dragged him to death through the streets. Also today: All the Saints of the Seraphic Order (Franciscans), and the vigil of Andrew.

Peter's brother, a fisherman of Bethsaida and a disciple of the Baptist, the first to be called — 'we have found the Messiah' — and the one who brought the boy with the loaves. Tradition sends him to Greece and Scythia and has him crucified at Patras on the X-shaped cross. Patron of Scotland, Russia, Greece and Constantinople. Advent begins on the Sunday nearest his feast.

The brilliant Oxford scholar who became a Jesuit, returned to England in disguise, printed his 'Brag' and the Ten Reasons, was betrayed, racked in the Tower and hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn with Ralph Sherwin and Alexander Briant. Also today: Eligius, the goldsmith-bishop, patron of metalworkers, and Charles de Foucauld.

A Roman girl scourged to death under Julian the Apostate after her parents and sister had been killed; her church on the Esquiline, rebuilt by Bernini, is the first he designed. Also today: Chromatius of Aquileia, friend of Jerome and Ambrose.

A Navarrese noble converted at Paris by Ignatius — 'what doth it profit a man?' — who sailed to Goa in 1541 and in ten years baptised tens of thousands in India, the Moluccas and Japan, then died on the island of Sancian within sight of China, which he could not enter. His body lies incorrupt in Goa; his arm in Rome.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: A Christian official of the caliph's court at Damascus who became a monk at Mar Saba and wrote the Fount of Knowledge, the first systematic theology, and the defence of holy images against the iconoclast emperors — beyond their reach under Muslim rule. Last of the Greek Fathers. Also today: Barbara, of the tower and the Holy Helpers.

A Cappadocian who founded the Great Lavra in the Kidron gorge below Bethlehem — Mar Saba, inhabited without interruption for fifteen centuries — and led the monks of Palestine in defence of Chalcedon. The Typikon of Mar Saba shaped the Byzantine office. Also today: Crispina of Numidia, martyr.

Bishop of Myra in Lycia, said to have thrown three bags of gold through a poor man's window to save his daughters from prostitution, to have calmed a storm, and to have struck Arius at Nicaea. His relics were carried off to Bari in 1087. Patron of children, sailors, Russia and Greece — and, by way of the Dutch Sinterklaas, Santa Claus.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: The Roman governor of Milan who entered the cathedral to calm a riot over the election of a bishop and heard a child cry 'Ambrose bishop!' — baptised, ordained and consecrated within a week. He barred the emperor Theodosius from church after the massacre of Thessalonica, introduced hymn-singing to the West, and baptised Augustine.

n: The Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: Mary, from the first instant of her conception, preserved free from original sin by the merits of her Son — 'Hail, full of grace' — defined by Pius IX in 1854 and confirmed, believers say, at Lourdes four years later. Patronal feast of the United States, Spain, Portugal, Brazil and the Philippines. A holy day of obligation.

An Aztec convert, a widower of fifty-seven, to whom the Virgin appeared on the hill of Tepeyac on 9 December 1531, speaking Nahuatl, and asked for a church; when the bishop demanded a sign, she filled his tilma with Castilian roses in winter, and her image appeared on the cloth. First indigenous saint of the Americas.

The Holy House of Nazareth, carried by angels (or, as records suggest, by the Angeli family of Epirus) to Loreto in 1294; the Litany of Loreto and the patronage of aviators come from it. Also today: Eulalia of Mérida, the twelve-year-old martyr of Spain, and the Martyrology's Melchiades, pope.

A Spanish-born pope who commissioned Jerome to revise the Latin Bible — the beginning of the Vulgate — restored the catacombs and wrote verse epitaphs for the martyrs, and obtained the emperor's recognition of Rome's primacy. His election was contested with bloodshed; his reign gave the Church its Bible.

The image on Juan Diego's tilma — a young woman, dark-skinned, pregnant, standing on the moon with the stars of the December sky of 1531 on her mantle — hangs in the basilica at Mexico City, the most visited Marian shrine in the world. Within a decade nine million Aztecs had been baptised. Patroness of the Americas and of the unborn.

A Sicilian of Syracuse who gave her dowry to the poor and was denounced by her suitor under Diocletian; the oxen could not drag her to the brothel, the fire would not burn her, and she died by the sword. Her name means light; she is shown with her eyes on a dish and crowned with candles in the Swedish midwinter. Named in the Roman Canon.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: The Carmelite friar who joined Teresa's reform, was kidnapped and imprisoned nine months in a cupboard at Toledo by his own order, escaped, and wrote the Dark Night of the Soul, the Spiritual Canticle and the Living Flame — the greatest mystical poetry in Spanish. 'In the evening of life, we shall be judged on love.'

Daughter of a rich Aachen manufacturer who founded the Sisters of the Poor of St Francis to nurse the sick in their homes; her sisters came to Cincinnati in 1858 and served both sides in the Civil War. Also today: Valerian of Abbenza, the aged bishop exiled by the Vandals.

Widow of the king of Italy, imprisoned by his successor, rescued by Otto the Great, who married her and made her empress; regent for her grandson Otto III, she founded Seltz abbey and died there. Odilo of Cluny wrote her life. Also today: the O Antiphons begin tomorrow — 'O Sapientia'.

Whom Jesus wept for and called out of the tomb after four days; Provence claims him as first bishop of Marseilles, Cyprus as bishop of Kition. Today begins the great O Antiphons of Advent: O Wisdom, O Adonai, O Root of Jesse, O Key of David, O Dayspring, O King of Nations, O Emmanuel.

First bishop of Killaloe in Ireland, son of a king of Thomond, who went to Rome to be consecrated by the pope; the Flannan Isles off Scotland bear his name. Also today: Gatian, first bishop of Tours, and Winebald of Heidenheim, brother of Willibald and Walburga.

A Benedictine canonist who as pope left Avignon for Rome in 1367 — the first to do so in sixty years — received the Byzantine emperor into the Church, founded universities, and, discouraged by Roman disorder, returned to Avignon, where he died within months as Bridget of Sweden had warned. Also today: Anastasius I, pope.

A Navarrese shepherd who became abbot of Silos in Castile and rebuilt its church and cloister, one of the glories of Romanesque sculpture; his staff was brought to Spanish queens in childbirth. Dominic Guzmán's mother named her son after him. Also today: Ursicinus of Saint-Ursanne.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: The Dutch Jesuit called 'the second apostle of Germany', who founded colleges from Prague to Fribourg and wrote the catechism that ran through two hundred editions in his lifetime and kept southern Germany Catholic. Also today, in the traditional calendar: Thomas the Apostle.
See November 13; she died on this day in Chicago in 1917. Also today: Chaeremon and Ischyrion, martyrs of Egypt under Decius, and the O Antiphon 'O Rex Gentium'.

A professor of theology at Kraków who gave his food and clothes to the poor, walked to Jerusalem and four times to Rome, and told his students, 'Fight all false opinions, but let your weapons be patience, sweetness and love.' Poland's saint of scholars. The last O Antiphon tonight: 'O Emmanuel'.

The Eastern calendars and old Western ones remember Adam and Eve on the eve of the Nativity: the first Adam and the first Eve on the day before the second are born. The paradise tree hung with apples in medieval plays for this day became the Christmas tree.

'And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.' The birth of Jesus at Bethlehem, kept on December 25 in Rome since at least 336, with three Masses — at midnight, at dawn and in the day. The Roman Martyrology's proclamation counts the ages of the world to this night; the Christmas season runs to the Baptism of the Lord.

One of the seven deacons, 'full of grace and fortitude', whose long speech before the Sanhedrin ended with the crowd stopping their ears; stoned outside Jerusalem while Saul held the coats, praying 'Lord, lay not this sin to their charge.' Good King Wenceslas looked out on his feast.

The disciple whom Jesus loved, who leaned on his breast at supper, stood at the cross and took Mary home, ran to the empty tomb, and — tradition says — survived the boiling oil at Rome, was exiled to Patmos, and died old at Ephesus, repeating 'Little children, love one another.' Wine is blessed on his day.

The boys of Bethlehem two years old and under, killed by Herod in his hunt for the newborn king — 'Rachel bewailing her children.' Martyrs not in will but in blood, the Church says; the day is kept in violet or rose, and in the Middle Ages a boy bishop ruled the cathedrals.

Henry II's boon companion and chancellor, who as archbishop of Canterbury turned against the king's control of the Church, spent six years in exile, and was cut down in his own cathedral by four knights who had taken the king's angry words for an order. Europe's most visited shrine until Henry VIII destroyed it; Chaucer's pilgrims were going there.

A bishop of Assisi who shattered a statue of Jupiter, had his hands cut off, and was beaten to death at Spoleto under Diocletian. Also today: Egwin of Worcester, founder of Evesham, and Anysia of Thessalonica, the girl killed by a soldier for refusing to sacrifice.

Pope through the reign of Constantine, when the Church came out of the catacombs: the Lateran, the Vatican basilica and Santa Croce were built, and the Council of Nicaea met, in his pontificate. The forged Donation of Constantine later made him the recipient of the Western Empire. New Year's Eve is 'Silvester' in half of Europe.
